stem: A client is receiving negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT). What is a primary action of this therapy?

options.A: Apply negative pressure to the wound and remove wound fluid/exudate
options.B: Deliver an antibiotic into the wound as the device's defining mechanism
options.C: Apply positive pressure to force wound edges apart
options.D: Seal the wound without creating suction or removing fluid

rationale: FDA device classification describes NPWT as applying negative pressure to a wound to remove fluids, including wound exudate. Current StatPearls also explains that negative pressure removes excess exudate and supports a wound-healing environment and granulation. Therefore A is the best answer. Antibiotic delivery is not the defining mechanism, positive pressure is the opposite mechanism, and NPWT uses active suction rather than a passive seal alone.
educational_objective: Explain that negative pressure wound therapy applies suction/negative pressure to the wound and removes exudate as part of wound management.
source_document_title: Product Classification — Negative Pressure Wound Therapy Powered Suction Pump (Product Code OMP)
source_version_date: FDA product-classification page current and accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Definition and Technical Method: powered suction pump for wound management via continual/intermittent negative pressure; suction creates a vacuum within the wound bed and pumps wound exudate into a collection canister
source_claim_supported: NPWT uses a powered suction pump to apply negative pressure to the wound and remove wound fluids/exudate.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort: provide nonpharmacological comfort measures, assist with therapies/devices, and provide skin/wound-related basic care as appropriate
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — wound-care device / negative pressure wound therapy
correction_summary: Replaced the generic FDA safety-communications locator with the current FDA device-classification page and limited the mechanism claim to what the device definition directly supports: negative pressure plus fluid/exudate removal. Removed the broader unsourced claim of improved blood flow and avoided making antibiotic delivery part of the mechanism.
audit_findings: A directly matches the FDA device definition and technical method. B, C, and D contradict the defining mechanism. The item does not require a pressure setting, dressing-change interval, or indication that would vary by device/wound. One best answer remains with direct wound-care relevance.
